summary: Redwood SE + AE ran a 58-minute deep dive with Cypher Dynamics on recurring KV-cache evictions that degrade long-context sessions. Discussed eviction heuristics, paging to host memory, prefix reuse patterns, batching/latency tradeoffs, and quantization impacts. Agreed to run an instrumented micro-benchmark and share detailed docs/configs; Redwood to propose pilot pricing for Dedicated capacity if needed.
topics: Prefix reuse and cache hit patterns
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 58m
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Carlos (CTO), Aisha (ML Infra), Liam (SRE)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I think we have about an hour, we'll go through the eviction behavior you've been seeing, priya will drive the tech bits. quick intros?
[00:18] Carlos: Yep, Carlos here, CTO at Cypher. We've been seeing a lot of long-context calls drop performance after ~1.5k tokens and the sessions start doing these large re-reads.
[00:28] Priya: hi team, I'm Priya on infra, SE from Redwood. we'll look at kv-cache architecture, eviction heuristics and how paging interacts with long context.
[00:36] Aisha: quick context, we're on a mix of hosted and on-prem nodes; for sensitive workloads we route to our VPC private cluster. saw eviction bursts both on hosted and our private cluster, but more frequent on the on-prem servers.
[00:50] Liam: and we see increased latency spikes coincident with eviction events, token rates drop, and sometimes generation repeats prefixes.

[03:05] Priya: okay, real quick recap of how our KV cache generally works: it's a per-model KV store that holds key-value pairs for cached transformer kvs so we don't recompute past activations. we use a hybrid eviction heuristic: LRU-ish with frequency weight and a working-set awareness that prefers keeping prefixes with high reuse. but under memory pressure we page older items to host memory (paging) and eventually evict.
[03:34] Carlos: so paging means moving from GPU to host RAM, not disk swap?
[03:38] Priya: yeah correct, host RAM first; we try to avoid disk unless the host is configured to allow swap/paging which we don't recommend for latency-sensitive workloads. sometimes your on-prem kernel settings force earlier paging.

[06:10] Liam: we instrumented a trace, there's a spike in "eviction_rate" right before clients see degraded outputs. there are also a lot of prefixes that look like near-duplicates, prefix-reuse is lower than we expect.
[06:23] Priya: that suggests the cache is getting fragmented across slightly different tokenizations or different prompt templates. prefix reuse is very sensitive: small changes in punctuation or system prompts lead to new cache entries and low hit rates.

[09:12] Jordan: are you doing prompt templating client-side? like dynamic user metadata inserted?
[09:18] Carlos: yes, we append session metadata (user id, last action) which probably creates many similar but distinct prefixes.
[09:25] Priya: that's the classic case — if you attach variable metadata to the start of the context you'll blow up the keyspace. fix options: 1) move mutable metadata to a separate, later step or 2) normalize templates / hash invariant fields before the model prompt so prefix reuse improves.

[12:00] Aisha: on the on-prem side we also had GPU memory fragmentation — long-running processes plus multiple small models pinned caused less contiguous free memory which triggered more aggressive paging. any recommendations?
[12:18] Priya: we recommend configuring the runtime with model pinning and active garbage collection windows: schedule evictions during low-traffic periods, increase contiguous allocation by using exclusive GPU assignment per model when feasible, and tune the kernel allocation flags. we sent a doc on our recommended nvml flags and CUDA behavior.

[16:04] Liam: what about quantization? we moved some models to int8 and some to int4 — does that change eviction thresholds?
[16:12] Priya: yes, quantization reduces per-kv size but also changes compute patterns; int4 may compress kvs aggressively so more entries fit but quantization artifacts can alter reuse if the model's tokenization or layer outputs slightly differ. as a rule: int8 gives predictable size/behavior, int4 is great for raw capacity but test thoroughly.

[19:30] Jordan: there's also batching impacts — customers often push up batch size to increase throughput and that increases concurrent prefix sets, increasing working set. any tradeoffs?
[19:42] Priya: batching improves GPU utilization but raises instantaneous working-set. if you combine large batch windows with long-context sessions, you multiply the KV retention needs. we suggest adaptive batching: lower batch windows for known long-context routes or pin those routes to Dedicated capacity.

[24:05] Carlos: we saw worse behavior when we used a shared hosted pool vs a dedicated node. is that expected?
[24:12] Priya: yes, shared pools are susceptible to noisy neighbors. Dedicated clusters reserve GPU pools, so your working-set is stable — fewer evictions. for regulatory reasons you mentioned earlier you might prefer private: in Private we can tune kernel selection and memory limits more aggressively.

[27:40] Liam: our logs show a lot of small eviction fragments: the cache evicts many small entries instead of a few big ones. is fragmentation a common cause?
[27:51] Priya: fragmentation plus non-uniform key sizes. keys for different layers can vary and without size-awareness the eviction policy can thrash. we have a size-aware eviction we can enable; it biases against evicting many small hot entries to free up space.

[31:10] Aisha: any quick checks we can run to validate the root cause?
[31:15] Priya: yes, instrument these metrics: cache_hits, cache_misses, eviction_rate_per_minute, paging_events, avg_kv_size, active_prefix_count, duplicate_prefix_rate. run a micro-benchmark that replays 1000 typical sessions and compare hits over time.
[31:40] Jordan: we'll provide a benchmarking plan doc (link: https://redwood.ai/docs/kv-cache-bench) and a sample script you can run in 30 minutes.

[34:58] Carlos: the paging_events in our on-prem graph correlate with a nightly batch job — maybe that job eats memory and triggers eviction for customer sessions.
[35:10] Priya: that's exactly the kind of pattern you want to avoid. isolate batch work to separate nodes or schedule outside peak sessions; on Private deployments we can provide node pools for batch jobs.

[39:20] Liam: about prefix reuse: we saw certain system messages that are almost identical but have different whitespace; is tokenization-level normalization worth it?
[39:33] Priya: yes normalize whitespace, stable system prompts, or use a prompt pre-hash to canonicalize repeated content. another trick is to aggregate mutable data into a single short placeholder token and expand it after generation.

[43:02] Jordan: security question — for Private clusters where eviction/paging touches host RAM, any data residency or encryption concerns?
[43:12] Priya: host RAM isn't persisted but if you page to disk you must ensure encrypted swap and adhere to your KMS/HSM policies. Redwood Private supports KMS integration and can disable swap entirely; we document audit log locations in the security pack. we'll share that.

[47:00] Carlos: will Dedicated guarantee less latency variance?
[47:06] Priya: yes, Dedicated reduces noisy neighbor effects and gives you stable working-set capacity; if you pin models and allocate a larger KV budget you'll see fewer evictions. SLA options apply (we have a Dedicated pilot) — Jordan can follow up on pricing.

[50:22] Aisha: any quick config flags we should try right away?
[50:28] Priya: enable size-aware-eviction=true, set kv_cache_max_entries to match your expected active_prefix_count * 1.5, set eviction_grace=30s to avoid thrashing on transient bursts, and increase host pinning for long-context models. sample configs in the doc.

[53:05] Carlos: about benchmarks: we'd like Redwood to run a small end-to-end bench on a mirrored dataset to prove fixes before we switch production — is that doable?
[53:15] Jordan: yes, pilot is standard. we can run a small benchmark on a Dedicated node for 2-3 days, instrument metrics, and provide a report. we'll include cost estimates.

[55:40] Priya: final quick notes: prefix reuse is the biggest lever; tooling to canonicalize prompts reduces eviction pressure immediately. combined with Dedicated capacity + size-aware eviction you'll likely get a big win. we'll send the exact steps and a preconfigured bench script.

[57:05] Jordan: recap and next steps: Priya shares docs + bench plan, Jordan sends pricing/pilot template, customer runs initial micro-bench and uploads traces. follow-up week of 2026-03-15. any last Qs?
[57:22] Carlos: nope thanks, that was helpful.
[57:26] Liam: thanks everyone.
[57:30] Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up.
